notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 23, but there are four gaps you should know about first:

- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I didn't find anything from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The only Catholic voice I have is Jerome, and he comes to me secondhand through the Pulpit Commentary.
- **Modern scholarship:** I found no bibleodyssey.org pages. From netbible.org I only got the NET translation of v. 13, not its notes.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
- **Methodist:** Adam Clarke appears only in short search excerpts, because his page and Gill's full page wouldn't load. I have little on v. 18 from Calvin (his comment on it wasn't in the part of the page I could read) and nothing on it from Gill or Clarke.

## Big-picture disagreement: which conquest does Isaiah mean?

This question shapes how you read several verses, so it comes first.
- **Calvin (Reformed):** It's Nebuchadnezzar, not Alexander. "he does not speak of Alexander, but of Nebuchadnezzar." His reason is that the prophecy promises Tyre will be restored, and Tyre was never restored after Alexander took it. He also says the point was to comfort the Jews: Tyre, which had oppressed them, would not escape punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/23.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** He agrees. Shalmaneser besieged Tyre but didn't take it. Nebuchadnezzar took it after a 13-year siege, and that is what's meant, because the 70 years that follow fit that period. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-23.html (excerpt only; full page wouldn't load)
- **Clarke (Methodist):** "This prophecy denounces the destruction of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-23.html (excerpt only)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Assyrian, Babylonian and Nebuchadnezzar captures were early, partial fulfilments, and "Alexander's destruction of the city was the final and complete fulfillment of the prophecy." It dates the oracle after 710 BC, when Sargon conquered Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Tyre had two parts. Assyria and Babylon conquered the mainland city, and Alexander took the island city in 332 BC, which he sees as a precise fulfilment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-23/
- **Ellicott:** He links the prophecy to Assyrian attacks. Ahaz's appeal to Tiglath-pileser had made Tyre a target too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html

## Verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik: Tyre was Phoenicia's leading city and the great sea power of the day, so its name stood for trade and materialism. He calls it the "Babylon of the Sea." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-23/
- Pulpit: The returning merchant fleet would stop at Cyprus and learn there that its home harbour was closed. "Tarshish" is probably Tartessus in Spain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- *Disagreement over Tarshish:* Clarke also says Tartessus in Spain (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-23.html). Calvin says the Hebrews called Cilicia "Tarshish" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/23.htm).
- Gill notes that the Puritan Cocceius read the whole prophecy as being about the antichristian city. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/23-1.html
- Background (Guzik): Tyre helped Israel when Hiram sent timber for the temple, but it also gave Israel Jezebel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-23/

**v. 2:** Pulpit: "Be still" means be silent, since complaining would do no good. Sidon's merchants were content to make Tyre rich. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Ellicott: Sidon, the older city, stands for Phoenicia as a whole. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html
- Calvin: The coastlands are told to be silent like people stunned by disaster. He compares the shock to what losing Venice or Antwerp would do to his own world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/23.htm

**v. 3:** Ellicott: Shihor ("the dark river") is the Nile. The grain trade with Egypt was a main part of Tyre's business, and Egypt's navy was in practice Phoenician. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html
- Pulpit: Egyptian grain was moved onto Phoenician ships at the Nile mouths. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Calvin: Isaiah praises Tyre's wealth so that its fall will more clearly be seen as God's work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/23.htm

**v. 4:** Ellicott: Sidon is spoken to as Tyre's mother city. The "fortress of the sea" is Tyre's island rock, now like a widow who has lost her children. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html
- Calvin: The "sea" is Tyre itself. The words mock her pride in colonies like Carthage, as if she had never borne children at all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/23.htm

**v. 5:** Pulpit: Egypt cared little for foreign nations, but Tyre's fall was a warning sign that the same power could come for Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Ellicott: Egypt needed Tyre to export its grain, and Tyre served as an outpost against Assyria. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html
- Calvin: Egypt is punished too, for pushing the Jews to rebel instead of trusting God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/23.htm

**v. 6:** Ellicott: This is sharp irony. Tyre's people must go to Tarshish as refugees, not as traders. When Alexander besieged Tyre, its people did send families to Carthage. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html
- Pulpit: When Sennacherib attacked, Sidon's king fled across the sea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm

**v. 7:** *Translation debate:* "Her feet carry her afar" could mean future exile or past colonising. Ellicott prefers the colonies reading and names Carthage as the chief one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html Pulpit lists scholars on both sides. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Calvin: Isaiah mocks Tyre's pride in being ancient and sets exile and poverty against it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/23.htm

**v. 8:** "Bestower of crowns": Ellicott says Tyre handed out crowns to its colonies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html Pulpit says the word must mean "crowning," not "crowned," and that "traffickers" is literally "Canaanites," a word that came to mean traders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Guzik: In Tyre money ruled. You didn't need royal birth or good character to be honoured, only business success. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-23/

**v. 9:** Guzik: Success made Tyre proud, so the Lord planned to humble it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-23/
- Pulpit: God isn't against beauty or glory as such. He opposes people who pride themselves in it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Ellicott: The verb means "to desecrate," possibly pointing to the destruction of Tyre's temples, such as Melkarth's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html
- Coffman: God condemns a false standard of success that honoured crooked traders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-23.html

**v. 10:** Ellicott and Pulpit: Tarshish and the other colonies are told to spread out like the Nile in flood. Tyre's "girdle," its restraint on them, is gone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm

**v. 11:** Pulpit: "He" is the LORD. "Canaan" means Phoenicia, which is why the Syro-Phoenician woman is called "a woman of Canaan." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Ellicott: The "shaking" reaches all the nations hit by Assyria's rise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html

**v. 12:** Ellicott: Tyre had never been conquered, a "virgin" fortress, and now that would change. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html
- Gill: "No more" means not for a long time, since after 70 years she sings again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-23.html
- Pulpit: Cyprus gave no safety. The Assyrians ruled it, and one fleeing Sidonian king was hunted down there and beheaded. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm

**v. 13:** This is the hardest verse in the chapter, and readings differ a lot.
- Pulpit: Babylon is held up as a warning. "He" is the Assyrian (Sargon, around 710 BC), and the point is: if Assyria did this to Babylon, think what it can do to you. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Older reading (Benson, Barnes, Gill): The Chaldeans were once a people of no account until Assyria settled them, yet they would be the ones to ruin Tyre. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/23-13.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/bible/ice/ilb/isaiah/23-13.html
- Calvin: "the daughter has devoured the mother," meaning Chaldea overthrew Assyria, and both would overthrow Tyre. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/23.htm
- Coffman (Church of Christ) accepts only the Babylonian reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-23.html
- Translations split too. RSV/NRSV read "This is the people; it was not Assyria. They destined Tyre for wild beasts." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/isaiah/23-13.html The NET has "these people who have lost their identity!" https://www.blueletterbible.org/net/isa/23/13/s_702013

**v. 14:** Pulpit: The poem ends where it began. "Strength" means the stronghold, Tyre itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Gill: Tyre was the safe port that held up the ships' whole trade. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-23.html

**v. 15:** Teachers disagree on the "seventy years."
- Constable lists four views: 70 literal years after Sennacherib in 701 BC; after Nebuchadnezzar; the same years as Israel's Babylonian exile (Delitzsch); or a round number. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/23-15.html
- Gill and JFB: The Babylonian kingdom lasted 70 years, and "one king" means a dynasty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/23-15.htm
- Clarke: The time given to the Babylonian empire. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-23.html
- Pulpit: A symbolic, indefinite number, like "forty years." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Ellicott follows Cheyne in reading it symbolically, counting from the Assyrian conquest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html
- Guzik takes it as an exact number decreed by God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-23/
- Gill also reports Jewish views: Rashi (Jarchi) thought "one king" meant David, and some take it as the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-23.html

**v. 16:** Guzik: Isaiah may be quoting a well-known song of his day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-23/ The Cambridge Bible on Bible Hub calls it a popular ballad. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/23-15.htm
- Calvin: The harp and sweet melody stand for merchants' tricks and flattery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/23.htm

**v. 17:** Gill and Pulpit: God "visits" Tyre in mercy, not judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/23-17.htm
- The "harlot" image is a picture of trade. The Cambridge Bible notes on that page say it highlights Tyre's money-driven dealings and compare Revelation 18:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/23-17.htm
- Ellicott: This was fulfilled when trade revived under the Persian kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-23.html

**v. 18:** Guzik: The riches Tyre chased end up given to the Lord anyway. Many see this fulfilled in the early church. Paul found believers in Tyre (Acts 21:4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-23/
- Pulpit: Jerome thought it hadn't happened yet in his day. If so, it may stand for business under Christianity paying for good works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/23.htm
- Restoration Commentary: Tyre's lasting legacy is believers like the Syro-Phoenician woman. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/isaiah-23.html
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) reads the chapter as God against exploitative commercial systems, linking it to Revelation 18. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/isaiah-23.html
